citation.title: Changing Climates of Conflict: A Social Network Experiment in 56 Schools

standing_assumptions:
The article (PNAS 113(3):566–571; printed pp. 566–571 are main PDF pp. 1–6) and its SI Appendix (43 pages; the printed page number equals the supplement PDF page number) state no theorem, proposition or lemma and give no proof. Their formal objects are the school-level regressions (SI Eqs. (1)–(6)), the exposure mapping, the exposure probabilities and the inverse-probability-weighted regression estimator (SI pp. 16–19), one sentence of asymptotic justification (SI p. 19) and the notes to Tables S6 and S7. There are two official corrections: PNAS 115(15):E3598 (2018), which replaces 30% by 25%, and a 2019 correction that adds a grant number. Everything quoted below was read from the rendered page images.
(S1) Schools and blocks. SI p. 5 (Study design): “Prior to randomization, schools agreed to participate in all measurement aspects of the program, with a 50% chance of receiving the anti-conflict program (the treatment).” “Schools were assigned to blocks of four, and randomized to receive the treatment or not within these blocks.” “Four schools dropped out from the study before the point of randomization, which left the total sample at 56 schools and 24,191 students.” Fig. S1, caption (SI p. 24): “The 56 schools were first blocked into groups of four by pretreatment school level variables including size and student demographics (see SI). Within each of the 14 school blocks, two schools were assigned to control (the two school networks on the left), and two to treatment, the anti-conflict intervention (the two school networks on the right). The nodes depict the population of students at the school. Grey nodes are the “seed eligible” students, selected by a deterministic algorithm and comprising a representative sample of the school. Seed eligibles were blocked into four equally sized groups based on pretreatment characteristics including gender and grade, and half of the students in each block were randomly assigned to be treated (part of the anti-conflict program) if they were in a treatment school; dark green nodes are treated seed eligibles. Nodes in the shape of stars are the social referents, who are in the top 10% of their school in connections reported by other students in the pre-randomization survey.”
(S2) Seed-eligibles and seeds. SI p. 6, with $a_i$ a student's indegree and $b_i$ the student's closure: “The students in each of the gender-grade-$b_i$ blocks with the largest values of $a_i$ were considered eligible for randomization into the seed group, such that we had no fewer than 40 seed-eligible students (schools with fewer than 200 students), and no more than 64 seed-eligible students (schools with less than 550 students). For schools with between 200 and 550, we scaled linearly between 40 and 64 seed-eligible students, rounding to the nearest 4. Table S2 demonstrates the covariate profiles of eligible and ineligible students. All of our estimates are computed conditional on the composition of the seed-eligible groups. Among treated schools, half of the seed-eligibles were block-randomized into the seed group, using 4 blocks constructed using gender, grade, and $b_i$ (using an R package, blockTools).” Main p. 567 (PDF p. 2): “In the 28 of 56 schools randomly assigned to receive the intervention, we selected a group of students (the seed-eligibles) using a deterministic algorithm (see SI Appendix for materials and methods used) designed to represent 15% of the school population, blocked by gender and grade and capped at 64 students (grades ranged from 5 to 8) (SI Appendix, Figs. S1 and S2, and Table S1). We randomly assigned 50% of that group (the seeds) to be invited to participate in the anticonflict intervention, which our team implemented over the course of the school year. Within each seed group at each school (on average 26 seeds at each school, for a total of 728 seeds across 28 schools), a random proportion were social referent seeds, meaning they were in the top 10% of their school in the number of connections reported by other students (i.e., indegree).”
(S3) School-level (climate) regressions. SI p. 13: “We fit the following linear regression model: $Y_{ij} = \alpha_j + \tau D_{ij} + \gamma C^E_{ij} + u_{ij}$ (1) where $ij$ denotes the $i$th school in the $j$th block. $Y_{ij}$ denotes school-level outcomes, $\alpha_j$ is a block-level fixed effect, $D_{ij}$ is the school-level treatment assignment, $C_{ij}$ is the composition of the seed group (percentage of seed group that is classified as a social referent), and $C^E_{ij}$ is the composition of the seed eligible group (percentage of seed eligible group that is classified as a social referent). $\tau$ here is the average causal effect of treatment. We include $C^E_{ij}$ as a covariate control here so as to maximize comparability with the interaction model in (4). In all cases, the model is fit with OLS regression with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors to characterize uncertainty.” The interaction model, Eq. (2) (repeated as Eq. (4)), and its interpretation are transcribed in P037-T14. SI p. 16: “This amounts to fitting the following model for main effects: $Y_{ij} = \alpha_j + \tau D_{ij} + \gamma C^E_{ij} + \boldsymbol{\theta}\mathbf{X}_{ij} + u_{ij}$, (5) where $\mathbf{X}_{ij}$ is a vector of school-specific pretreatment covariates (percentage white, percentage English-speaking, average house quality and, where available, pretreatment measurement of $Y_{ij}$).” Main p. 568 (PDF p. 3): “We computed confidence intervals and P values using robust SEs under a normal approximation.” Main p. 567: “(Administrative data were available for 49 of the 56 schools, and we restricted our attention to these schools for analyses of conflict-related events.)”
(S4) Scale of composition. In the targets $C_{ij}$ and $C^E_{ij}$ are fractions in $[0,1]$ (0.20 means 20%), the scale of Fig. 2 and Table S7. The SI's wording (“percentage”, “$c\%$”, “percentage points”) does not match that scale; this is finding P037-N020, rated a clarity note, and is not a target.
(S5) Social-influence setting. SI pp. 16–17: “We have a finite population of students indexed by $i = 1, ..., N$ on which our randomized experiment is performed. Define a treatment assignment vector, $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, ..., z_N)'$, where $z_i \in \{0, 1\}$ denotes whether or not student $i$ is assigned to be a seed (i.e., is invited to participate in the anti-conflict group). An experimental design is a plan for randomly selecting a particular value of $\mathbf{z}$ with predetermined probability $p_{\mathbf{z}}$. Restricting our attention only to treatment assignments that can be generated by our experimental design, define $\Omega = \{\mathbf{z} : p_{\mathbf{z}} > 0\}$, so that $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, ..., Z_N)'$ is a random vector with support $\Omega$ and $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = p_{\mathbf{z}}$. In this setting, treatment assignment is the random assignment of seeds both across and within schools according our hierarchical randomization (i.e., so that half of schools are assigned to control schools with no seeds).” The exposure mapping $f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i)$ with $\theta_i$, $\gamma$ and $s_i$ (SI p. 17) is transcribed in P037-T7. SI p. 18: “We allow for each student $i$ to have a vector of potential outcomes, which we denote by $(y_i(d_C), ...y_i(d_D))$, that do not depend on the value of $\mathbf{Z}$. We seek estimates for $k \in \{C, S, NI, I\}$ (i.e., control exposure, school exposure, non-social referent peer exposure, social referent peer exposure) of the average potential outcome $\mu(d_k) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k)$.” “$\pi_i(d_k) = \sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\Omega} \mathbf{I}(f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i) = d_k)\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})$.” “We restrict ourselves to the subpopulation of students (n=2451) for which there exists some probability that students could receive all four exposures: $0 < \pi_i(d_k) < 1$ for $k \in \{C, S, NI, I\}$.” The estimator $\widehat{\mu_R}(d_k)$ (SI p. 19) is transcribed in P037-T11.
(S6) None of the eleven headline claims (P037-H1 to P037-H11) is a mathematical statement: each is an empirical estimate, a description of the design or an interpretive conclusion. Every target below therefore comes from a confirmed error.
(S7) [Added on 6 October 2026, after the authors' analysis code became available; it applies to the revised P037-T2 and to P037-T18 onward.] The authors' eleven R scripts, as released by ICPSR with study 37070, were not available when (S1)–(S6) and P037-T1 to T17 were written. In the targets added or revised afterwards, ‘the released code’ means those scripts as read and run by the checkers; a statement of what the code does is established by the code and is not a statement of the publication. ‘On the public data’ means a value obtained from the public data release (ICPSR 37070 V2) run through the authors' scripts with an adapter, or from a reconstruction on that release; the authors' own analysis files are not public and ICPSR states that some variables in the release were changed, so such a value is not the value the authors would obtain from their own files. No such value is part of a target's statement: the statements are exact identities, probabilities, counts and counterexamples, and values on the public data appear only in notes, as aggregates (the data are respondent-level records of school students; no respondent row and no school identifier is given). The scripts are cited by number: script 1, ‘1. Sanitize and generate perms, probs.R’ (the network, referent status, the simulated seed and school assignments, the exposure indicators and their simulated probabilities); script 2, ‘2. Cleaning.R’ (outcomes and covariates); script 3, ‘3. Network results.R’ (the social-influence estimates and their randomization standard errors); script 4, ‘4. School results-with-correction.R’ (the school-level regressions, their three kinds of standard error, the percentages of the 2018 Correction and Fig. 2); script 6, ‘6. Bond et al analysis.R’ (Fig. S5). Line numbers are those of the released files, as cited by the checkers.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Tables S6 and S7, the rows ‘Bayesian Bootstrap SE’ and the sentence of each note that describes them, as printed
canonical_claim.location: SI Appendix, Table S6, p. 41, and Table S7, p. 42 (supplement PDF pp. 41–42)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Table S6, SI p. 41] “Table S6. Average school-level climate effects caused by anti-conflict groups.” Columns: Friends talk about conflict | Prescriptive norms | Wristband | Peer conflict. School level main effect: $0.09$ | $-0.01$ | $0.16$ | $-0.06$. Heteroskedasticity Robust SE: $(0.02)$ | $(0.08)$ | $(0.01)$ | $(0.03)$. Bayesian Bootstrap SE: $(0.01)$ | $(0.05)$ | $(0.01)$ | $(0.03)$. Wild Bootstrap SE: $(0.02)$ | $(0.08)$ | $(0.01)$ | $(0.03)$. Note: “Regression-based estimates of mean differences between treatment and control schools. Estimates computed using ordinary least squares with covariate controls and fixed effects for randomization block. Standard errors are reported in parentheses. Bayesian bootstrap standard errors generated using 5,000 replicates, applying weights to each school drawn from the standard uniform distribution. Wild bootstrap standard errors generated using 5,000 replicates, multiplying residuals by draws from the standard normal distribution.”
[Table S7, SI p. 42] “Table S7. Average school-level climate effects caused by anti-conflict groups, interacted with proportion of social referent seeds in the group.” Same columns. School effect with 0% Social Referents: $0.08$ | $0.05$ | $0.15$ | $0.04$. Heteroskedasticity Robust SE: $(0.03)$ | $(0.15)$ | $(0.02)$ | $(0.07)$. Bayesian Bootstrap SE: $(0.03)$ | $(0.11)$ | $(0.02)$ | $(0.05)$. Wild Bootstrap SE: $(0.03)$ | $(0.14)$ | $(0.02)$ | $(0.07)$. Interaction: Proportion of Referents in Treatment group: $0.10$ | $-0.53$ | $0.12$ | $-0.85$. Heteroskedasticity Robust SE: $(0.29)$ | $(1.06)$ | $(0.18)$ | $(0.46)$. Bayesian Bootstrap SE: $(0.22)$ | $(0.80)$ | $(0.13)$ | $(0.35)$. Wild Bootstrap SE: $(0.30)$ | $(1.07)$ | $(0.18)$ | $(0.47)$. Note: “Regression-based estimates of the effects of treatment conditional on the proportion of social referent seeds in the group, under a linear approximation. “School effect with 0% Social Referents” refers to the estimated value of treatment when the group contains no Social Referents. “Interaction: Proportion of Referents in Treatment groups” refers to the first derivative of the effect size with respect to the percentage of the group that were referents. Estimates computed using ordinary least squares with covariate controls and fixed effects for randomization block. A control is also included for the expected value of the seed group composition in the school (over all possible randomizations). Standard errors are reported in parentheses. Bayesian bootstrap standard errors generated using 5,000 replicates, applying weights to each school drawn from the standard uniform distribution. Wild bootstrap standard errors generated using 5,000 replicates, multiplying residuals by draws from the standard normal distribution. A graphical version of this table is presented in Figure 2 in the main text of the paper.”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The regressions are SI Eqs. (5) and (6) (standing assumption (S3); P037-T14), with the school as the unit. The paper defines neither ‘Bayesian bootstrap’ nor how the weights enter the refits; the validator's definition and reading are in P037-T4. The tables are printed sideways on the page.
canonical_claim.note: Listed because finding P037-E005 (Moderate) touches it and the brief asks for the statement as printed. The rows are reported numbers and the note is a description of a procedure; the only formalizable content is the identification the note makes, namely that weights drawn independently from the standard uniform distribution, one per school, are Bayesian-bootstrap weights, that is, that after normalization they have the $\mathrm{Dirichlet}(1,\dots,1)$ law. P037-T4 refutes that for every number of schools from two up. Lean cannot decide what the authors' code did, nor whether the twelve entries are too small; if nothing can be stated beyond the identification that P037-T4 refutes, not_applicable is the right status. For the record, the six cells of Table S7 in which the Bayesian-bootstrap and robust entries differ have ratios $\tfrac{22}{29}$, $\tfrac{11}{15}$, $\tfrac{40}{53}$, $\tfrac{13}{18}$, $\tfrac57$, $\tfrac{35}{46}$ (0.71 to 0.76); Sol does not accept these as evidence of the algorithm used.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Abstract, Significance statement, Results (first paragraph) and Discussion: the reduction of disciplinary reports ‘by 30%’, as printed
canonical_claim.location: main p. 566 (PDF p. 1), p. 569 (PDF p. 4) and p. 571 (PDF p. 6)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Abstract, p. 566] “Compared with control schools, disciplinary reports of student conflict at treatment schools were reduced by 30% over 1 year.”
[Significance, p. 566] “By encouraging a small set of students to take a public stance against typical forms of conflict at their school, our intervention reduced overall levels of conflict by an estimated 30%.”
[Results, p. 569] “In a control school, we estimated that each student in the school was officially disciplined for peer conflict on average 0.20 times per year. We estimated an average decrease of 0.06 disciplinary events per student in treatment schools, a 30% reduction in peer conflict reports.”
[Discussion, p. 571] “By seeding the network with students who were encouraged to take a public stance against typical forms of conflict at their school, our intervention reduced overall levels of disciplinary reports of peer conflict by an estimated 30% over 1 y. To put this in perspective, our estimates imply that the intervention reduced the total number of disciplinary events from 2,695 events to 2,012 events across the 11,938 students in treatment schools.”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: As for P037-T6. The 2018 Correction (p. E3598), which replaces 30 by 25 at these four places, is transcribed in P037-T15. Table S6 (SI p. 41) reports the school-level main effect on peer conflict as $-0.06$ with each of its three standard errors $(0.03)$ (P037-T16).
canonical_claim.note: Listed because finding P037-N001 (Moderate) touches it and the brief asks for the statement as printed. The four sentences report an empirical estimate. Their formalizable content is arithmetic: in Results, $0.06/0.20 = \tfrac3{10}$, which is true of the two printed numbers (P037-T6 (v)); in the Discussion, that a reduction from 2,695 to 2,012 events is a reduction of 30%, which is false, since $\tfrac{683}{2695}$ rounds to 25% (P037-T6 (i)–(iii)). Lean cannot decide the size of the true effect. If nothing can be stated beyond P037-T6, not_applicable is the right status. The significance statement that accompanies the Results sentence is P037-T3 and P037-T15; the 2018 Correction already repairs the percentage.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Main Methods, ‘We computed confidence intervals and P values using robust SEs under a normal approximation’, with the heteroskedasticity-robust Wald tests of Results (first paragraph) and of the Fig. 2 caption and the rows ‘Wild Bootstrap SE’ of Tables S6 and S7, corrected: what the released procedure computes (the HC0 variance with a normal reference), that the wild bootstrap as coded has exactly the HC0 covariance, and that HC0 is biased downward under homoskedastic errors by an amount fixed by the leverages
canonical_claim.location: main p. 568 (PDF p. 3); main p. 569 (PDF p. 4), Results and Fig. 2 caption; SI p. 13 (supplement PDF p. 13); SI Tables S6 and S7, pp. 41–42 (supplement PDF pp. 41–42)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] The passages are transcribed in P037-T37 (the two test statements also in P037-T15, the table rows and notes in P037-T16). [Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P037-N006), its first and last sentences, verbatim] “Specify HC0 and the unadjusted residual-normal bootstrap, and qualify the finite-sample uncertainty using the demonstrated calibration failures.” “A calibrated replacement uncertainty procedure for the original average-effect and interaction claims remains unestablished; a retreat from significance wording alone does not repair that procedural defect.”
[Mathematical content, from the adjudicating session's derivation (materials-adj, decision.md, ‘Complete covariance derivation and fresh calibration experiments’).] Setting: $n$ schools; $X$ the $n \times k$ design matrix of full column rank $k$ (the nonaliased columns of Eq. (5) or (6): block indicators, $D_{ij}$, $C_{ij}D_{ij}$ where present, $C^E_{ij}$ and the covariates); $y$ the vector of school outcomes; $A = (X'X)^{-1}X'$; $H = XA$ with diagonal entries $h_{ii}$; $\hat b = Ay$; $e = (I - H)y$ the residuals.
(a) [The variance estimator of the released code.] $\hat V_{\mathrm{HC0}} = A\,\mathrm{diag}(e_1^2,\dots,e_n^2)\,A' = (X'X)^{-1}X'\mathrm{diag}(e_i^2)X(X'X)^{-1}$. The standard error of coefficient $j$ is $s_j = \sqrt{(\hat V_{\mathrm{HC0}})_{jj}}$ and the two-sided normal Wald $P$ value is $2\,(1 - \Phi(|\hat b_j|/s_j))$. No factor $n/(n-k)$ and no leverage correction enters.
(b) [The wild bootstrap as coded has the HC0 covariance exactly.] Let $v = (v_1,\dots,v_n)'$ be random multipliers, independent of the data, with $\mathrm{E}[v] = 0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(v) = I_n$ (in the code, independent standard normal draws), and put $y^* = X\hat b + \mathrm{diag}(e)\,v$ and $b^* = Ay^*$. Then $b^* = \hat b + A\,\mathrm{diag}(e)\,v$, $\mathrm{E}[b^* \mid X, y] = \hat b$ and $\mathrm{Var}(b^* \mid X, y) = A\,\mathrm{diag}(e_i^2)\,A' = \hat V_{\mathrm{HC0}}$. So the standard deviation of a coefficient over the bootstrap replicates estimates its HC0 standard error, and the bootstrap carries no finite-sample adjustment.
(c) [Leverages.] $H$ is symmetric and idempotent, $0 \le h_{ii} \le 1$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{n}h_{ii} = k$; the mean leverage is $k/n$.
(d) [HC0 is biased downward under homoskedastic independent errors.] Suppose $y = X\beta + u$ with $\mathrm{E}[u \mid X] = 0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(u \mid X) = \sigma^2I_n$. Then $e = (I - H)u$, $\mathrm{E}[e_i^2 \mid X] = \sigma^2(1 - h_{ii})$, $\mathrm{Var}(\hat b \mid X) = \sigma^2AA' = \sigma^2(X'X)^{-1}$, $\mathrm{E}[\hat V_{\mathrm{HC0}} \mid X] = \sigma^2A\,\mathrm{diag}(1 - h_{ii})\,A'$, and $\mathrm{Var}(\hat b \mid X) - \mathrm{E}[\hat V_{\mathrm{HC0}} \mid X] = \sigma^2A\,\mathrm{diag}(h_{ii})\,A'$, which is positive semidefinite. For coefficient $j$, with $a_{ji}$ the entries of row $j$ of $A$ (and $\sigma^2 > 0$), $$\frac{\mathrm{E}[(\hat V_{\mathrm{HC0}})_{jj} \mid X]}{\mathrm{Var}(\hat b_j \mid X)} = \frac{\sum_i a_{ji}^2(1 - h_{ii})}{\sum_i a_{ji}^2} = 1 - \frac{\sum_i a_{ji}^2h_{ii}}{\sum_i a_{ji}^2} \le 1,$$ with equality only if $h_{ii} = 0$ for every $i$ with $a_{ji} \ne 0$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: From the paper: main p. 568, ‘We computed confidence intervals and P values using robust SEs under a normal approximation’; SI p. 13, ‘In all cases, the model is fit with OLS regression with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors to characterize uncertainty’; the models with covariates, SI Eqs. (5) and (6) (standing assumption (S3); P037-T14); the notes to Tables S6 and S7, ‘Wild bootstrap standard errors generated using 5,000 replicates, multiplying residuals by draws from the standard normal distribution’ (P037-T16). The paper does not name the variant of the heteroskedasticity-robust estimator and states no test other than the Wald test. Established from the released code (standing assumption (S7)): script 4, lines 162–163 and 208–209, calls vcovHC with type = "HC", which is HC0; lines 178–195 and 228–248 form the bootstrap outcomes from the raw, unscaled residuals times independent normal draws and take the standard deviation of the refitted coefficients over 5,000 draws; the script prints coefficients and standard errors and no $P$ value, so the two-sided normal Wald $P$ value of (a) is the checkers' reading of main p. 568. Not in the paper: $A$, $H$, the leverages $h_{ii}$, and the benchmark of (d) (independent errors with a common variance), which is the validator's and is not an assumption of the paper, whose stated basis for the school-level estimates is the randomization of schools. $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function.
canonical_claim.note: P037-N006 is rated an error, Major (ratings.json; it was undetermined before the code was available). Sol's verdict is confirmed in part, adjudicated between two sessions; both falsity flags are null, because the Methods sentence describes the procedure accurately and claims no exact size; repair cost no_repair_known (no calibrated replacement procedure is established). There is no counterexample target: the exact rational witness in the artifacts (an estimate $-\tfrac{649}{10000}$ with HC0 standard error $\tfrac{251}{10000}$, which print as $-0.06$ and $0.03$ and keep a normal $P$ value below 0.05 after the HC1 factor at ranks 19 and 20) refutes a claim of the raisers (that the HC1 factor alone removes significance for every pair compatible with Table S6) and not a statement of the publication. What a proof establishes: (a)–(d), identities of linear algebra and of second moments; in particular the row ‘Wild Bootstrap SE’ is not a check on the robust row that is independent of it, and the robust variance is too small in expectation in the homoskedastic benchmark by the factor of (d). Established only by rerun or simulation on the public data (ICPSR 37070 V2 run through the authors' scripts with an adapter), and so not part of the target: the conflict regressions use 49 schools and have ranks $k = 19$ and $20$ (the pretreatment outcome is constant and aliased), so the mean leverages of (c) are $\tfrac{19}{49}$ and $\tfrac{20}{49}$; the ratios of (d) are 0.619 for the treatment coefficient of Eq. (5) and 0.556 for the interaction coefficient of Eq. (6); in 100,000 Gaussian null draws on those two designs the nominal 5% test rejects in 13.7% and 16.0%; in 30,000 two-of-four re-randomizations under the sharp null of no effect it rejects in 13.0% and 12.4%, and the randomization $P$ values of the observed statistics are about 0.20 and 0.15; the main effect is $-0.0573$ (HC0 SE 0.0347, two-sided normal $P = 0.099$) and the interaction $-0.841$ (SE 0.463, $P = 0.069$). The public data reproduce the Table S6 coefficient and standard error at printed precision and give $-0.84$ where Table S7 prints $-0.85$; the authors' own files are not public, so these are not the values the authors would obtain from them. What a proof does not establish: the rejection probability of the test under the design, a calibrated replacement (Sol: HC1 or HC2 with a $t$ reference still over-reject in the Gaussian benchmark, and the sharp-null randomization test addresses a stronger null), or that a printed $P$ value is wrong on the authors' files. The conflict between the Results sentence and the 2018 Correction is P037-N008 (P037-T3, T15); the uniform-weight rows are P037-E005 (P037-T4, T5, T16).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Fig. 2, caption and panel keys (‘Control schools' predicted mean (and 95% CI)’, ‘Treatment schools' predicted mean (and 95% CI)’; ‘95% confidence intervals estimated using heteroskedasticity-robust SEs for the regression fit’), and the school-level panels of Fig. S6; the released code draws the treatment band from the standard error of a contrast and the control band from a residual variance divided by 56. An exact data set in which both differ from the robust variance of the predicted mean (the validator's certificate; not in the paper)
canonical_claim.location: main p. 569 (PDF p. 4), Fig. 2; SI Appendix p. 33 (supplement PDF p. 33), Fig. S6
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact data set of 56 schools in which the two band constructions of the released code give variances different from the heteroskedasticity-robust (HC0) variances of the two predicted means that the caption and the panel keys name (the validator's certificate; not in the paper).
[Data] 56 schools in six groups of identical rows (number of schools; treatment $T$; composition $C$; outcome $Y$): $(14;\ 0;\ 0;\ 0)$, $(14;\ 0;\ 0;\ \tfrac15)$, $(7;\ 1;\ 0;\ \tfrac1{10})$, $(7;\ 1;\ 0;\ \tfrac3{10})$, $(7;\ 1;\ \tfrac15;\ \tfrac25)$, $(7;\ 1;\ \tfrac15;\ \tfrac35)$; 28 control and 28 treated schools.
[Fit] $Y = \alpha + \tau_0T + \beta\,TC + e$ by OLS (the interaction model without block indicators and covariates); the design has rank 3.
Claims.
(i) $(\hat\alpha, \hat\tau_0, \hat\beta) = (\tfrac1{10}, \tfrac1{10}, \tfrac32)$, and every residual is $\tfrac1{10}$ or $-\tfrac1{10}$.
(ii) The HC0 covariance matrix of $(\hat\alpha, \hat\tau_0, \hat\beta)$ is $$\hat V = \begin{pmatrix}\tfrac{1}{2800} & -\tfrac{1}{2800} & 0\\ -\tfrac{1}{2800} & \tfrac{3}{2800} & -\tfrac{1}{280}\\ 0 & -\tfrac{1}{280} & \tfrac{1}{28}\end{pmatrix}.$$
(iii) [The quantities named in the figure.] At $c = \tfrac1{10}$, with $\ell_0 = (1,0,0)$, $\ell_1 = (1,1,\tfrac1{10})$ and $d = \ell_1 - \ell_0 = (0,1,\tfrac1{10})$: the control predicted mean is $\ell_0\hat b = \tfrac1{10}$, the treatment predicted mean is $\ell_1\hat b = \tfrac7{20}$ and their difference is $d\hat b = \tfrac14$; $\ell_0\hat V\ell_0' = \tfrac1{2800}$, $\ell_1\hat V\ell_1' = \tfrac1{2800}$, $d\hat Vd' = \tfrac1{1400}$ and $\ell_0\hat Vd' = -\tfrac1{2800}$, in agreement with $\ell_1\hat V\ell_1' = \ell_0\hat V\ell_0' + d\hat Vd' + 2\,\ell_0\hat Vd'$.
(iv) [The treatment band of the code.] The regression of $Y$ on $1$, $T$ and $T(C - \tfrac1{10})$ has the same residuals, its coefficient on $T$ is $\hat\tau_0 + \tfrac1{10}\hat\beta = \tfrac14$, and the HC0 variance of that coefficient is $\tfrac1{1400} = d\hat Vd'$. The code places $\pm 1.96$ times the square root of this number round the treatment predicted mean; the variance of that mean is $\tfrac1{2800}$, one half of it.
(v) [The control band of the code.] The 28 control residuals are fourteen times $-\tfrac1{10}$ and fourteen times $\tfrac1{10}$; their mean is $0$ and their sample variance is $s^2 = \tfrac{28/100}{27} = \tfrac{7}{675}$. The code uses the variance $s^2/56 = \tfrac{1}{5400}$, whereas $\ell_0\hat V\ell_0' = \tfrac1{2800}$; the ratio is $\tfrac{14}{27}$.
Hence in this data set the treatment band is wider and the control band narrower than the 95% intervals of the predicted means: neither construction is the robust interval of the quantity it is drawn round.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: From the paper: the caption of Fig. 2 and the keys of its panels, and the caption of Fig. S6 (transcribed in P037-T40); the interaction model, SI Eq. (2) (repeated as (4)) and, with covariates, Eq. (6) (P037-T14); main p. 568, ‘We computed confidence intervals and P values using robust SEs under a normal approximation’. HC0: for a regression with design matrix $X$ and residuals $e_i$, $\hat V = (X'X)^{-1}X'\mathrm{diag}(e_i^2)X(X'X)^{-1}$ (P037-T18 (a)); the robust variance of a linear combination $\ell\hat b$ is $\ell\hat V\ell'$. canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] The captions and panel keys are transcribed in P037-T40. [Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P037-N026), verbatim] “Redraw the bands using mhat_g(c) +/- 1.96*sqrt(l_g(c)' V_HC0 l_g(c)), where the averaged prediction design row and covariance matrix come from the same model and retained sample as the line. Remove the mismatched centered-refit SE and residual-variance/56 constructions. The caption can then retain its stated interpretation as approximate pointwise intervals.”
[Mathematical content, from the validator's derivation (v1, sections 1–3).] Setting: the $n$ schools of the fit that produces a plotted line; design matrix $X$ of full column rank with columns $1$, $T$, $TC$ and nuisance columns $z$ (the block indicators but one, $C^E$, the covariates); OLS coefficient $\hat b = (\hat\alpha, \hat\tau_0, \hat\beta, \hat\eta')'$ with residuals $e_i$; $\hat V = (X'X)^{-1}X'\mathrm{diag}(e_i^2)X(X'X)^{-1}$ its HC0 covariance; $\bar z$ the average nuisance row over the retained schools. For a composition $c$ put $\ell_0 = (1, 0, 0, \bar z')$, $\ell_1(c) = (1, 1, c, \bar z')$ and $d(c) = \ell_1(c) - \ell_0 = (0, 1, c, 0')$.
(a) [The plotted levels.] The control predicted mean is $\hat m_0 = \ell_0\hat b$, the treatment predicted mean is $\hat m_1(c) = \ell_1(c)\hat b$, and $\hat m_1(c) - \hat m_0 = d(c)\hat b = \hat\tau_0 + c\hat\beta$.
(b) [Corrected bands.] The pointwise 95% intervals of the two predicted means under the paper's normal approximation are $\hat m_0 \pm 1.96\sqrt{\ell_0\hat V\ell_0'}$ and $\hat m_1(c) \pm 1.96\sqrt{\ell_1(c)\hat V\ell_1(c)'}$.
(c) [Mean variance against contrast variance.] $\ell_1(c)\hat V\ell_1(c)' = \ell_0\hat V\ell_0' + d(c)\hat Vd(c)' + 2\,\ell_0\hat Vd(c)'$. So $d(c)\hat Vd(c)'$ equals the variance of the treatment predicted mean exactly when $\ell_0\hat V\ell_0' + 2\,\ell_0\hat Vd(c)' = 0$, and it can be larger or smaller.
(d) [What the centred refit of the code computes.] For fixed $c$ the regression with columns $1$, $T$, $T(C - c)$, $z$ on the same schools has the same fitted values and residuals as the original one; its coefficient on $T$ is $\hat\tau_0 + c\hat\beta$, and the HC0 variance of that coefficient is $d(c)\hat Vd(c)' = \hat V_{\tau\tau} + 2c\,\hat V_{\tau\beta} + c^2\hat V_{\beta\beta}$, the variance of the treatment-control contrast at composition $c$, where $\hat V_{\tau\tau}$, $\hat V_{\tau\beta}$, $\hat V_{\beta\beta}$ are the entries of $\hat V$ for $(\hat\tau_0, \hat\beta)$.
(e) [The control band of the code.] With $e_i$ the residuals of the $n_0$ control schools of the fit and $s^2_{e,0} = \frac{1}{n_0 - 1}\sum_{i : T_i = 0}(e_i - \bar e_0)^2$, the number $s^2_{e,0}/56$ is not $\ell_0\hat V\ell_0'$ in general (P037-T23 (v)); replacing 56 by $n_0$ does not make it so in general.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Main Methods, the sentence on the 49 schools, and the Fig. 1 caption, corrected: the rule by which the released code selects the schools of the conflict analyses, and the condition on that rule under which the selected analysis keeps its causal reading
canonical_claim.location: main p. 567 (PDF p. 2); Fig. 1 caption, main p. 568 (PDF p. 3); SI Appendix p. 10 (supplement PDF p. 10)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] The passages are transcribed in P037-T38. [Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P037-N007), verbatim] “State: 'The released code constructs each student's peer-conflict outcome by summing DE4-DE16, DE46, DE47, HIBO and HIBT after replacing missing category counts by zero, and retains schools whose student mean exceeds 0.02. On ICPSR 37070 V2 after the released row screen, this selects 49 schools (26 control, 23 treatment), although 52 schools (26 in each arm) have recorded conflict fields. The three further exclusions have recorded discipline fields; this release alone does not establish the completeness or usability of their original peer-conflict records.' Keep 49 as the code-derived analysis count; do not equate all seven public threshold exclusions with absence of records.” [Sol's repair-cost note, the sentences on the further condition, verbatim] “None applies to that descriptive repair only: preserving causal estimands or inference after an outcome-dependent screen would require an additional unverified condition such as assignment-invariant selection/reporting, or a justified alternative analysis. Complete reporting alone does not supply that condition, as the saved exact counterexample proves.”
[Mathematical content, from the checker's derivation (doubt, derivation.md, section 5).] Setting: a finite set of units $i$ (schools, or students), a random assignment $Z$ with finite support $\Omega$, an exposure $D_i = D_i(Z)$ with $\pi_i(d) = \Pr(D_i = d)$, fixed potential outcomes $y_i(d)$, and an inclusion indicator $A_i(Z) \in \{0,1\}$. In the released code, for the conflict analyses, $A_i(Z) = \mathbf{1}\{\bar Y_{s(i)}(Z) > \tfrac{1}{50}\}$, where $\bar Y_s(Z)$ is the mean of the recorded conflict count over the students of school $s$ under assignment $Z$ and $s(i)$ is the school of unit $i$.
(a) [Assignment-invariant inclusion.] If $A_i(Z) = a_i$ for every $Z \in \Omega$, then for every exposure $d$ with $\pi_i(d) > 0$, $\mathrm{E}\big[a_i\,\mathbf{1}\{D_i = d\}\,y_i(d)/\pi_i(d)\big] = a_i\,y_i(d)$. Hence, if $\pi_i(d) > 0$ for every kept unit and $n_a = \sum_ia_i > 0$, $\mathrm{E}\big[n_a^{-1}\sum_ia_i\,\mathbf{1}\{D_i = d\}\,y_i(d)/\pi_i(d)\big] = n_a^{-1}\sum_{i : a_i = 1}y_i(d)$, the mean potential outcome of the kept population.
(b) [Assignment-dependent inclusion.] In general, for $\pi_i(d) > 0$, $\mathrm{E}\big[A_i(Z)\,\mathbf{1}\{D_i = d\}\,y_i(d)/\pi_i(d)\big] = y_i(d)\,\Pr(A_i(Z) = 1 \mid D_i = d)$, and the factor $\Pr(A_i(Z) = 1 \mid D_i = d)$ may differ between exposures $d$ and between units.
(c) [A sufficient condition for the threshold rule.] If for every school $s$ the mean $\bar Y_s(Z)$ lies on the same side of $\tfrac{1}{50}$ for every $Z \in \Omega$ (either $\bar Y_s(Z) > \tfrac1{50}$ for all $Z$, or $\bar Y_s(Z) \le \tfrac1{50}$ for all $Z$), then $A_i(Z)$ does not depend on $Z$ and (a) applies. This holds in particular under the sharp null hypothesis that the recorded outcome of every student is the same under every assignment.
(d) [Randomization, complete reporting and a constant effect do not imply the condition.] In the design of P037-T19 the condition of (c) fails for one school, $\Pr(A_1 = 1 \mid D_1 = 1) = 1$ and $\Pr(A_1 = 1 \mid D_1 = 0) = 0$, and the selected difference in means and the selected block regression have expectation $\tfrac{3}{200}$ and limit $\tfrac{3}{250}$ where the effect is $\tfrac{3}{100}$.

The weighting of (a) and (b) is the paper's inverse-probability weighting in its simplest form (SI pp. 18–19; standing assumption (S5)), with $y_i(d_k)$ fixed and $\pi_i(d_k) > 0$; for the school-level analyses the exposure is the school's treatment, $d \in \{0,1\}$, with $\pi_i(d) = \tfrac12$. ‘Assignment-invariant selection/reporting’ in Sol's wording is the hypothesis of (a): the kept set is the same for every assignment in the support. (W1) [Positive probability against the cutoff 0.01.] One seed block has 12 eligible students, numbered $0,\dots,11$, of whom 6 are drawn (one of $\binom{12}{6} = 924$ equally likely selections, independent of the school's treatment). canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Main Methods, SI pp. 14, 18–19 and the note to Table S5, the population of the social-influence estimates, corrected: the analysis set of the released code, and how it stands to the positive-probability population
canonical_claim.location: main p. 568 (PDF p. 3); SI Appendix pp. 14, 18 and 19 (supplement PDF pp. 14, 18, 19); Table S5 note, SI p. 40
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] The passages are transcribed in P037-T39. [Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P037-N025), verbatim] “Replace the common support-population/N description with the actual outcome-specific restriction: all four estimated probabilities >0.01, observed nonseed status, available outcome and preprocessed preY, and peer-conflict school mean >0.02; state that predictions are averaged over this same set. Remove the shared n=2,451 and report original-run outcome-specific Ns if recovered. Do not substitute public-rerun Ns as original Ns.”
[Mathematical content.] Notation of standing assumption (S5). Let $K = \{C, S, NI, I\}$; for a student $i$ and $k \in K$ let $\pi_{ik} = \pi_i(d_k)$ and let $\hat\pi_{ik} = \frac1J\sum_{\ell=1}^{J}\mathbf{I}[f(\mathbf{z}^{\ell},\theta_i) = d_k]$ be the frequency of exposure $d_k$ in $J\ge1$ assignments $\mathbf{z}^1,\dots,\mathbf{z}^J \in \Omega$ (the corrected formula of P037-T9). Define the sets
$$P = \{i : 0 < \pi_{ik} < 1\ \forall k \in K\},\quad T = \{i : \pi_{ik} > \tfrac{1}{100}\ \forall k \in K\},\quad \hat P = \{i : \hat\pi_{ik} > 0\ \forall k \in K\},\quad \hat T = \{i : \hat\pi_{ik} > \tfrac{1}{100}\ \forall k \in K\},$$
and, for an outcome $o$ and the realized assignment $\mathbf{Z}$, the analysis set of the released code
$$M_o(\mathbf{Z}) = \{i \in \hat T : Z_i = 0,\ \text{the outcome } o \text{ and the pretreatment score of } i \text{ are available, and, for peer conflict, the school of } i \text{ passes the screen of P037-T20}\}.$$
(a) $P = \{i : \pi_{ik} > 0\ \forall k \in K\}$, because the five mutually exclusive and exhaustive exposure probabilities satisfy $\sum_{k\in K}\pi_{ik}+\pi_i(d_D)=1$, so $\sum_{k\in K}\pi_{ik}\le1$, and positivity of the other indirect exposures forces each $\pi_{ik}<1$; and $T \subseteq P$.
(b) [Simulated frequencies give no false positives.] If $\pi_{ik} = 0$ then $\hat\pi_{ik} = 0$ for every sequence of assignments from $\Omega$. Hence $\hat T \subseteq \hat P \subseteq P$ for every such sequence, and $M_o(\mathbf{Z}) \subseteq P$.
(c) [The inclusions are strict in general.] There are designs of the paper's form with a student in $P \setminus T$, and sequences of 10,000 assignments with that student in $\hat P \setminus \hat T$ (P037-T21 (W1)).
(d) [The cutoff is applied to a random quantity.] Let $J = 10{,}000$ and let the assignments be independent draws from the design. For a student of $P$ and $k \in K$, $J\hat\pi_{ik}$ has the binomial law with parameters $10{,}000$ and $\pi_{ik}$, the event $\hat\pi_{ik} > \tfrac1{100}$ is the event that exposure $d_k$ occurs at least 101 times among the draws, and $0 < \Pr(\hat\pi_{ik} > \tfrac1{100}) < 1$. claim_correction.problem: The paper describes one positive-probability population of 2,451, while the released-code rule also uses estimated cutoffs, realised nonseed status, available outcomes and baselines, and the school screen. That discrepancy survives, but clause (e)’s heading and inference do not follow from positive seed probability alone: another condition can exclude a student for every assignment. For the legal W2 focal student, make its outcome always unavailable and retain an observed never-seed background student with passing simulated cutoffs; then M_o(z) is a constant singleton for every supported z even though the focal seed probability is 1/4. A constant set is still a measurable random set, so this refutes necessary nonconstant membership, not measurability or the seed-exclusion probability bound.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: SI Appendix, the precision of the simulated exposure probabilities, corrected: the exact law of the estimate for a fixed number of draws, and the sense in which increasing the number of draws gives arbitrary accuracy
canonical_claim.location: SI Appendix p. 14 and p. 18 (supplement PDF pp. 14 and 18)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, SI p. 14] “We achieve an arbitrarily precise estimate of $\pi_i$ via $J = 10,000$ simulated random assignments of $\mathbf{Z}$ according to the experimental design:” (the formula that follows is transcribed, as printed, in P037-T9). [Printed, SI p. 18] “We can achieve an arbitrarily precise estimate of $\pi_i$ via simulated random assignments of $\mathbf{Z}$ according to the experimental design:” (the same formula) “Aronow [52] provides details on the rate of convergence of the estimated probabilities. In our study, we use $J = 10,000$ replicates of the administration of treatment assignments to estimate the $\pi_i(d_k)$ values.”
[Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P037-N021), its first sentence, verbatim] “Replace the fixed-J precision sentence with: "We estimate exposure probabilities from J=10000 simulated assignments; increasing J can make the Monte Carlo approximation arbitrarily accurate at any prescribed confidence level."”
[Mathematical content, from the validator's derivation (v1, sections 2, 4–6).] Fix a student $i$ and an exposure $d_k$, put $p = \pi_i(d_k)$, let $\mathbf{Z}^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf{Z}^{(J)}$ be independent draws from the design and $\hat\pi = \frac1J\sum_{\ell=1}^{J}\mathbf{I}[f(\mathbf{Z}^{(\ell)},\theta_i) = d_k]$ (the corrected formula of P037-T9).
(a) [Exact law.] $J\hat\pi$ has the binomial law with parameters $J$ and $p$: $\mathrm{E}[\hat\pi] = p$, $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\pi) = p(1-p)/J$ and $\Pr(\hat\pi = 0) = (1-p)^J$.
(b) [A fixed $J$ does not give arbitrary precision.] $\hat\pi$ takes its values in $\{0, \tfrac1J, \dots, 1\}$. If $0 < p < \tfrac{1}{2J}$, then $|\hat\pi - p| \ge p$ for every outcome of the simulation. If $0 < p < 1$, then $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\pi) > 0$.
(c) [Increasing $J$.] For every $\varepsilon > 0$, $\Pr(|\hat\pi - p| \ge \varepsilon) \le \dfrac{p(1-p)}{J\varepsilon^2} \le \dfrac{1}{4J\varepsilon^2}$; so for $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\delta > 0$ the bound is at most $\delta$ as soon as $J \ge \dfrac{1}{4\delta\varepsilon^2}$. For $m$ pairs of a student and an exposure, $\Pr(\max|\hat\pi - p| \ge \varepsilon) \le \dfrac{m}{4J\varepsilon^2}$.
(d) [Estimated positivity errs on one side only.] If $p = 0$ then $\hat\pi = 0$ for every sequence of assignments from $\Omega$; if $0 < p < 1$ then $\Pr(\hat\pi = 0) = (1-p)^J > 0$. So the rule ‘every estimated probability is positive’ can leave out a student all of whose probabilities are positive and cannot admit a student one of whose probabilities is zero.
(e) [The probability of school exposure under the blocked seed design.] For a student who is not eligible, in a school treated with probability $\tfrac12$ whose seed blocks $b$ have $n_b$ eligibles of whom $t_b$ are drawn uniformly, independently across blocks, and who has $m_b$ peers among the eligibles of block $b$: $$\pi_i(d_S) = \frac12\prod_b\frac{\binom{n_b - m_b}{t_b}}{\binom{n_b}{t_b}},$$ with $\binom{a}{t} = 0$ for $a < t$. With four blocks, $n_b = 10$ and $t_b = 5$: the peer counts $(2,2,2,2)$ give $\tfrac{8}{6561}$, $(5,3,0,0)$ give $\tfrac{1}{6048}$, $(6,2,0,0)$ give $0$ and $(5,5,0,0)$ give $\tfrac{1}{127008}$ (the witness of P037-T29).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: As for P037-T29 and P037-T9. The repaired sentence keeps $J = 10{,}000$ as what the study used; in the released code (standing assumption (S7)) script 1, lines 24–25 and 208–214, draws 10,000 assignments and averages the draw-specific exposure indicators. In (e) a peer is a student connected to the focal student in the peer relation used for exposure (P037-T26), and an eligible focal student would add itself to the count of its own block; (e) is used here only for a student who is not eligible. The independence of the draws is used in (a), in the second clause of (b), in (c) and in the second clause of (d).
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (b): if $r = J\hat\pi = 0$ the error is $p$; if $r \ge 1$ it is at least $\tfrac1J - p > p$ when $p < \tfrac{1}{2J}$. (c) is Chebyshev's inequality with $p(1-p) \le \tfrac14$, and a union bound over the $m$ pairs. (e): in block $b$ the seeds must be drawn from the $n_b - m_b$ eligibles that are not peers, which happens for $\binom{n_b - m_b}{t_b}$ of the $\binom{n_b}{t_b}$ selections. The only limit statement is the remark, implied by (c), that the estimate converges in probability to $p$ as $J \to \infty$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: SI Appendix, ‘simulated random assignments of $\mathbf{Z}$ according to the experimental design’ (pp. 14 and 18) and ‘1,000 simulated randomizations (both randomization across schools and within seed-eligibles)’ (pp. 19–20); in the released code the simulated school assignments are 28 of the 56 schools drawn without the blocks. Exact differences between that law and the design of two schools in each block of four (the validators' computations; not in the paper)
canonical_claim.location: SI Appendix pp. 14, 18 and 19–20 (supplement PDF pp. 14, 18, 19, 20); the design is on SI p. 5 and in Fig. S1, SI p. 24
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact differences between the law of the school assignments simulated by the released code and the law of the experimental design (the validators' computations; not in the paper).
[The two laws] 56 schools in 14 blocks of four; $S = (S_1,\dots,S_{56}) \in \{0,1\}^{56}$ with $S_h = 1$ when school $h$ is treated. $P_B$ (the design): uniform on the assignments with exactly two treated schools in every block. $P_U$ (the released sampler): uniform on the assignments with exactly 28 treated schools.
Claims.
(i) [Supports.] $P_B$ has $6^{14} = 78{,}364{,}164{,}096$ equally likely assignments and $P_U$ has $\binom{56}{28} = 7{,}648{,}690{,}600{,}760{,}440$; every assignment of the design is possible under $P_U$, and the $P_U$-probability that a draw respects all 14 blocks is $\dfrac{6^{14}}{\binom{56}{28}} = \dfrac{9795520512}{956086325095055}$ (about $1.02 \times 10^{-5}$).
(ii) [Marginals.] $P_B(S_h = 1) = P_U(S_h = 1) = \tfrac12$ for every school.
(iii) [Pairs.] For two different schools $h \ne j$: under $P_B$, $\Pr(S_h = S_j = 1) = \tfrac16$ if they are in the same block and $\tfrac14$ if not; under $P_U$, $\Pr(S_h = S_j = 1) = \tfrac{28\cdot27}{56\cdot55} = \tfrac{27}{110}$ for every pair. The covariances of $S_h$ and $S_j$ are $-\tfrac1{12}$ (same block) and $0$ (different blocks) under $P_B$, and $-\tfrac1{220}$ for every pair under $P_U$.
(iv) [Eight schools in two blocks of four.] There are $\binom84 = 70$ assignments with four treated schools and $\binom42^2 = 36$ with two treated schools in each block; 34 assignments of the first kind, for example $(1,1,1,1,0,0,0,0)$, are impossible under the blocked design. The probability that two schools are both treated is $\tfrac3{14}$ for every pair under the unblocked law, and $\tfrac16$ (same block) or $\tfrac14$ (different blocks) under the blocked law.
(v) [The variance of a statistic can move either way.] Let $n = 2m$ schools have fixed outcomes $y_h$, the same under treatment and control, and let $T = \frac1m\sum_h(2S_h - 1)\,y_h$ be the difference between the mean outcome of the treated and of the control schools. Under either law $\mathrm{E}[T] = 0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(T) = \frac{1}{m^2}\sum_h\sum_jy_hy_j\,\mathrm{E}[R_hR_j]$ with $R_h = 2S_h - 1$, $\mathrm{E}[R_h^2] = 1$ and $\mathrm{E}[R_hR_j] = 4\Pr(S_h = S_j = 1) - 1$ for $h \ne j$. For 56 schools: if $y$ equals 1 on the four schools of one block and 0 elsewhere, $\mathrm{Var}_U(T) = \tfrac{13}{2695}$ and $\mathrm{Var}_B(T) = 0$; if $y$ equals $1$ and $-1$ on two schools of one block and 0 elsewhere, $\mathrm{Var}_U(T) = \tfrac{1}{385}$ and $\mathrm{Var}_B(T) = \tfrac{1}{294}$. For eight schools: $y = (1,1,1,1,0,0,0,0)$ gives $\tfrac17$ unblocked and $0$ blocked; $y = (2,0,1,1,1,1,1,1)$ gives $\tfrac17$ unblocked and $\tfrac16$ blocked.

Sol's verdict is confirmed, by two validators, and the rater's doubt was settled by a measurement on the public data; evidence type exact_counterexample (sections 2–4 of the first validator's derivation; exact_output.txt and exact_results.json in the same folder; the doubt session's derivation, sections 2–3). canonical_claim.name_in_paper: SI Appendix, the simulated randomizations ‘according to the experimental design’, corrected: the law of the school assignments that the simulations must draw from, what is unchanged when the blocks are omitted (each student's exposure probabilities) and what is not (the joint law across schools)
canonical_claim.location: SI Appendix pp. 14, 18 and 19–20 (supplement PDF pp. 14, 18, 19, 20); the design is on SI p. 5
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, SI p. 5] “Schools were assigned to blocks of four, and randomized to receive the treatment or not within these blocks.” [Printed, SI pp. 14 and 18] The estimate of $\pi_i$ is obtained ‘via ... simulated random assignments of $\mathbf{Z}$ according to the experimental design’ (the two sentences are transcribed in P037-T30). [Printed, SI pp. 19–20] “Randomization-based confidence intervals for average potential outcomes are obtained under a maintained hypothesis of constant effects. Specifically, we use 1,000 simulated randomizations (both randomization across schools and within seed-eligibles) to estimate the standard errors under the maintained hypothesis that, for all $i$, $y_i(d_k) = y_i(D_i) + \hat\mu_R(d_k) - \hat\mu_R(D_i)$.”
[Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P037-N031), verbatim] “Replace script 1 line 58 by sch.perms <- genperms(schtreat, blockvar = schrb, clustvar = schid, maxiter = niter); regenerate exposure matrices and recompute network SEs, confidence intervals and Wald P values. Since exact marginal pi_i(d_k) are invariant for this school-local graph, common fixed marginal weights can also isolate the inference correction without resimulating those weights.”
[Mathematical content, from the validators' derivations (v1, sections 2–3; doubt, sections 2–3).] 56 schools in blocks $B_1,\dots,B_{14}$ of four; $S_a \in \{0,1\}$ the treatment of school $a$; $P_U$ the uniform law on the assignments with exactly 28 treated schools, which is the law of the released sampler (P037-T31).
(a) [The law of the design.] $P_B(S = s) = 6^{-14}\prod_{b=1}^{14}\mathbf{1}\{\sum_{a \in B_b}s_a = 2\}$: the 14 blocks are independent and within a block the six pairs of treated schools are equally likely. Simulated assignments ‘according to the experimental design’ are draws of $S$ from $P_B$ together with the within-school seed draws, which are independent of $S$.
(b) [Uniform choice of $m$ of $n$.] If $m$ of $n$ schools are chosen uniformly, $\Pr(S_h = 1) = \tfrac mn$ and, for $h \ne j$, $\Pr(S_h = S_j = 1) = \tfrac{m(m-1)}{n(n-1)}$: $\tfrac12$ and $\tfrac16$ for $(n,m) = (4,2)$; $\tfrac12$ and $\tfrac{27}{110}$ for $(n,m) = (56,28)$.
(c) [Each student's exposure probabilities do not depend on the blocks.] Let $U_a$ be the vector of the seed selections that school $a$ would receive if treated, drawn independently of $S$, so that $Z_i = S_{a(i)}U_i$ for a student $i$ of school $a(i)$. Suppose the exposure of student $i$ is a function $f_i(S_{a(i)}, U_{a(i)})$ of the treatment and the seed selections of its own school only (no peer relation between schools). Then for every law $L$ of $S$ that is independent of the $U_a$ and has $\Pr_L(S_a = 1) = \tfrac12$, $$\pi_{i,L}(d_k) = \tfrac12\Pr\big(f_i(0, U_{a(i)}) = d_k\big) + \tfrac12\Pr\big(f_i(1, U_{a(i)}) = d_k\big);$$ in particular $\pi_{i}(d_C) = \tfrac12$ and $\pi_i(d_k) = \tfrac12\Pr(f_i(1, U_{a(i)}) = d_k)$ for $k \ne C$. So $\pi_{i,B}(d_k) = \pi_{i,U}(d_k)$ for every student and exposure, and the positive-probability population and the estimands $\mu(d_k)$ are the same under $P_B$ and $P_U$.
(d) [The joint law across schools does depend on the blocks.] For students $i$, $i'$ in two different schools of one block, $\Pr(D_i = d_C,\ D_{i'} = d_C) = \Pr(S_{a(i)} = S_{a(i')} = 0) = \tfrac16$ under $P_B$ and $\tfrac{27}{110}$ under $P_U$; for schools in different blocks the values are $\tfrac14$ and $\tfrac{27}{110}$. Hence the randomization distribution of a statistic that combines schools, and its variance, differ under the two laws, with no general direction (P037-T31 (v)).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: As for P037-T31. $D_i = f(\mathbf{Z},\theta_i)$ is the exposure of student $i$ and $d_C$ the control exposure, $1 - s_i = 1$ (SI p. 17; P037-T7, P037-T8). The hypothesis of (c), that exposure depends on the student's own school only, holds for the exposure mapping of the paper when no student has a peer in another school; in the released code the peer relation is built within schools, and the validators found no tie between schools in the network reconstructed from the public data. (c) concerns the exact probabilities; two finite sets of 10,000 draws give different estimates of them. In (d), $\Pr(S_h = S_j = 0) = \Pr(S_h = S_j = 1)$ under both laws, by the symmetry between treated and control schools.

Two exact networks in which the nomination row and the union row give different exposures and different exposure probabilities (the checker's certificates; not in the paper)
canonical_claim.location: SI Appendix p. 17 (supplement PDF p. 17); main p. 567 (PDF p. 2) and p. 568 (PDF p. 3)
canonical_claim.statement:
Two exact networks in which student $i$'s row of the nomination matrix and student $i$'s row of the either-direction matrix give different exposures (the checker's certificates; not in the paper).
[Notation] $B_{ij} = 1$ if student $i$ nominated student $j$ and $0$ otherwise ($B_{ii} = 0$); $S_{ij} = \mathbf{I}(B_{ij} + B_{ji} > 0)$. The indegree of $j$ is $\sum_iB_{ij}$, and $\gamma_j = 1$ when the indegree of $j$ is in the top decile of its school; in both certificates the referents are the students whose indegree is above the school's 90th percentile (linear interpolation between order statistics), no student having an indegree equal to it. For a student who is not a seed, in a treated school, with $t$ the number of its peers that are seeds and $r$ the number of its referent peers that are seeds: the exposure is $d_S$ if $t = 0$, $d_{NI}$ if $t > 0$ and $r = 0$, and $d_I$ if $r > 0$ (the conditions of main p. 568; the corrected mapping of P037-T8).
(W1) A school of ten students $1,\dots,10$ whose only nominations are $2 \to 1$, $3 \to 2$ and $4 \to 2$. The indegrees are $(1,2,0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0)$, the 90th percentile is $\tfrac{11}{10}$, and student 2 is the only referent. Let the school be treated, student 2 the only seed, and consider student 1. With $\theta_1$ the first row of $B$: $(t, r) = (0, 0)$ and the exposure is $d_S$. With $\theta_1$ the first row of $S$: $(t, r) = (1, 1)$ and the exposure is $d_I$.
(W2) A school of twenty students $1,\dots,20$ whose only nominations are $2 \to 1$, $1 \to 3$, $1 \to 5$, $i \to 2$ for $i = 9,\dots,14$ and $i \to 3$ for $i = 15,\dots,20$. The indegrees are 1 for student 1, 6 for student 2, 7 for student 3, 1 for student 5 and 0 otherwise; the 90th percentile is $\tfrac32$; the referents are students 2 and 3. Student 1 has $\{3, 5\}$ as its row of $B$ and $\{2, 3, 5\}$ as its row of $S$. Design: the school is treated with probability $\tfrac12$ and, if it is treated, three seeds are drawn uniformly from $\{2,3,5,6,7,8\}$ (20 equally likely sets); student 1 is never a seed.
(i) Of the 20 seed sets, with the row of $B$: 4 give $d_S$, 6 give $d_{NI}$ and 10 give $d_I$; with the row of $S$: 1 gives $d_S$, 3 give $d_{NI}$ and 16 give $d_I$.
(ii) $(\pi(d_C), \pi(d_S), \pi(d_{NI}), \pi(d_I)) = (\tfrac12, \tfrac1{10}, \tfrac3{20}, \tfrac14)$ with the row of $B$ and $(\tfrac12, \tfrac1{40}, \tfrac3{40}, \tfrac25)$ with the row of $S$.
(iii) Under both readings all four probabilities lie strictly between 0 and 1, so student 1 belongs to the positive-probability population under both, with different probabilities of three of the four exposures, hence different inverse-probability weights.
So the printed sentence does not determine the exposure, its probabilities or the analysis population until the matrix is named, and positivity, the top-decile rule for referents and the design do not make the two readings agree.

canonical_claim.note: P037-N032 is rated an error, Moderate (ratings.json). Sol's verdict is confirmed in part, after the rater's doubt was settled (it was not confirmed before); false as printed: no; false under the natural reading: yes. What is confirmed is an omitted definition: the printed row and count identities hold when $\theta_i$ is the row of the either-direction matrix, and a reader of the SI and of main p. 567 naturally takes the row to be the student's own nominations. The certificates are in section C, step 8, of the checker's derivation (exact_certificate.json in the same folder). They are synthetic and do not reproduce the eligibility algorithm; setting all potential outcomes to zero shows that the constant-effects hypothesis does not remove the difference either. What a proof establishes: the two readings define different exposure mappings, probabilities and weights. What it does not establish (Sol): that any published estimate changes, that either reading is the right model of attention, or what the original analysis used (the authors' own files are not public). canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] The passages are transcribed in P037-T41. [Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P037-N032), verbatim] “For the primary social-influence analyses, peers are connected when either student nominated the other before treatment. Let B_ij indicate the directed nomination relation and S_ij=I(B_ij+B_ji>0); theta_i is the i-th row of S for both observed labels and random-assignment exposure probabilities. Referent status gamma is computed from directed indegree in the nomination graph; the betweenness variation substitutes its directed-graph centrality indicator. Separately, the Fig.S5 alternative statistic uses students nominated by each seed or unselected seed-eligible student, retaining the listed recipient occurrences, rather than the primary either-direction relation.”
[Mathematical content, from the checker's derivation (doubt, derivation.md, section C).] Let $B$ be an $N \times N$ matrix with entries in $\{0,1\}$ and zero diagonal ($B_{ij} = 1$ when student $i$ nominated student $j$), $S_{ij} = \mathbf{I}(B_{ij} + B_{ji} > 0)$, $\mathbf{z} \in \{0,1\}^N$ an assignment and $\gamma \in \{0,1\}^N$.
(a) $S$ has entries in $\{0,1\}$, is symmetric and has zero diagonal; $S_{ij} \ge B_{ij}$; and $M = S - B$ has entries in $\{0,1\}$, with $M_{ij} = 1$ exactly when $j$ nominated $i$ and $i$ did not nominate $j$.
(b) [Corrected definition.] $\theta_i = (S_{i1},\dots,S_{iN})'$, the $i$th row of $S$. Then $\mathbf{z}'\theta_i = \sum_jS_{ij}z_j = (S\mathbf{z})_i$ is the number of seeds $j$ such that $i$ nominated $j$ or $j$ nominated $i$ (a reciprocal pair counted once), and $(\mathbf{z}\circ\gamma)'\theta_i = \sum_jS_{ij}z_j\gamma_j = (S(\mathbf{z}\circ\gamma))_i$ is the number of those seeds that are referents; this holds for every $\mathbf{z}$ and every $\gamma$.
(c) With $c_i = (B\mathbf{z})_i$, $b_i = (M\mathbf{z})_i$, $r_i = (B(\mathbf{z}\circ\gamma))_i$ and $q_i = (M(\mathbf{z}\circ\gamma))_i$ (nonnegative integers with $r_i \le c_i$ and $q_i \le b_i$): $(S\mathbf{z})_i = c_i + b_i$ and $(S(\mathbf{z}\circ\gamma))_i = r_i + q_i$.
(d) [When the two rows give the same exposure.] For a student who is not a seed, in a treated school, the exposure computed from the $i$th row of $B$ and the exposure computed from the $i$th row of $S$ (by the three conditions $t = 0$; $t > 0$ and $r = 0$; $r > 0$ on the number $t$ of seed peers and the number $r$ of referent seed peers) are equal if and only if $(c_i > 0 \text{ or } b_i = 0)$ and $(r_i > 0 \text{ or } q_i = 0)$. In particular they are equal for every assignment of the design when $M_{ij}z_j = 0$ for every $j$ and every $\mathbf{z} \in \Omega$, that is, when every nomination received by $i$ from a student who can be a seed is returned.
(e) [Direction of the change.] For such a student and every $\mathbf{z}$: if the exposure from the row of $S$ is $d_S$, the exposure from the row of $B$ is $d_S$; if the exposure from the row of $B$ is $d_I$, the exposure from the row of $S$ is $d_I$. Hence, writing $\pi^B_i$ and $\pi^S_i$ for the exposure probabilities under the two definitions, $\pi^S_i(d_S) \le \pi^B_i(d_S)$ and $\pi^S_i(d_I) \ge \pi^B_i(d_I)$, with strict inequality as soon as one assignment of $\Omega$ changes the exposure from $d_S$, respectively to $d_I$.
(f) [The two definitions differ in general.] P037-T25.

canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (d), by cases: if $c_i = 0$ then $r_i = 0$ and the exposure from $B$ is $d_S$, while the exposure from $S$ is $d_S$ exactly when $b_i = 0$ (and then $q_i = 0$); if $c_i > 0$ and $r_i = 0$ the exposure from $B$ is $d_{NI}$, and the exposure from $S$ is $d_{NI}$ exactly when $q_i = 0$; if $r_i > 0$ both are $d_I$.
